fieldMarks: Stout toad 50-100 mm (usually about 75 mm) with thick, warty skin; brown, olive, grey or reddish, changing with temperature, humidity and stress.
Dark spots on the back each contain only one or two warts, sometimes ringed with white or yellow; oval pupils with a gold ring.
Males have dark (black or brown) throats; females are larger with white throats; belly white or yellow.
Toxic milky skin secretions irritate eyes and mouths.
behavior: Mainly nocturnal and most active in warm humid weather; by day hides under rocks and logs or digs into leaf litter and soil, backing in; digs deeper to hibernate.
Call is a long trill lasting 4-20 seconds, given by males at breeding ponds in late spring and early summer.
Eats a wide range of invertebrates (beetles, slugs, snails, earthworms), up to about 1,000 insects a day; tadpoles graze algae.
habitat: Terrestrial apart from a short breeding season; occupies forests to prairies wherever moisture, food and a breeding site are available; breeds in shallow, slow or still water, often with few fish.
range: NatureServe lists it across eastern and central North America: Labrador, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Nunavut, Ontario, Prince Edward Island and Québec, and most of the eastern and central US; Newfoundland is listed as introduced.

lookalikes.name: Southern toad
lookalikes.howToTell: Southern has high cranial crests with pronounced knobs between and behind the eyes, which American lacks.

lookalikes.name: Fowler's toad
lookalikes.howToTell: Fowler's has three or more warts in each dark back spot and a mostly unspotted belly with a single dark chest spot; American has one or two warts per spot.
